# RoboPuppy – project reference

Starting point for each Claude conversation. Updated at the end of every session.

## Goal
A Labrador-sized robotic dog built from 3D-printed and laser-cut parts. The robot is designed around its actuators. It must be able to trot dynamically.

**CAD tool: SolidCraft.** The model is generated by Node scripts (see Tooling).

## Requirements (from the owner)
- Torso about 60 cm long; everything else scaled to an average dog of that size.
- Legs: 3 axes each (hip abduction, hip pitch, knee).
- Head: 2 axes. Tilt is at the base of the neck (the whole neck nods); pan is at the top of the neck. Neck is short (about 92 mm).
- Tail: 2 axes (wag and lift), both at the tail root.
- Empty bay in the middle of the torso for battery and electronics (contents decided later).
- Exposed mechanical look for now; no cosmetic body shell.
- Fabrication available: FDM printer with 300 mm+ bed, laser cutter (wood/acrylic), and metal/carbon sheet through an external service.

## Decisions so far
- **Leg actuators:** 12× RobStride 02, classic CAN version (owner's decision, 2026-11-21; replaces the RobStride 01). 17 N·m peak, 6 N·m rated, about 405 g, Ø78.5 × 45.5 mm, 48 V rated, 24–60 V range, 410 rpm no-load at 48 V. It has the same front face and output flange as the RS01, but a bigger, longer rear cover and a different rear screw-head layout. Its speed advantage over the RS01 comes only from the higher voltage. It costs about the same as the RS01 from the sellers found. Accepted budget is roughly EUR 1,600–1,900 for all actuators. The CAD uses the RS02 (`robstride02.sc`, checked against the official STEP file). Its power connector is two XT30(2+2) sockets in the rear-cover rim, pointing outward on opposite sides; the model carries an estimated keep-out for each mated plug. Comparison of all RobStride models, prices and the CAN vs CAN FD reasoning: `docs/robstride_comparison.md`.
- **Head and tail actuators:** four Feetech STS-family serial bus servos (STS3215 class for head pan and both tail axes, a stronger one of the same size for neck tilt). Modelled as 45 × 24.7 × 35 mm bodies from memory of the datasheet; dimensions not yet verified. They need about 12 V, so a step-down converter from the battery, rated for 60 V or higher input.
- **Neck:** tilt servo lies on top of the deck at the front (ahead of the hip carriers' sweep); a printed neck (yoke, 45 mm tube at 45°, cradle) carries the pan servo.
- **Head:** hollow printed shell (skull 110 × 100 × 85, muzzle 95 × 56 × 48, 2.5 mm walls) on the pan servo horn. One camera behind each eye, 64 mm apart; keep-out sized for a Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 (assumption until the computer is chosen). The rest of the head is left empty for future additions.
- **Tail:** wag servo hangs under the rear tip of the deck spine with its shaft up through the deck; it carries the lift servo; the tail is a flexible 300 mm TPU rod on a yoke.
- **Leg architecture:** abduction actuator fixed to the torso; hip-pitch actuator held in a printed carrier; knee actuator on the thigh, coaxial with the hip pitch, driving the knee through a 1.5:1 belt (HTD 5M, 15 mm wide, 635 mm long, 24:36 teeth) between two thigh plates. The shank blade swings beside the belt, not in its plane.
- **Thigh plates:** 3 mm aluminium, laser-cut (owner's choice for now; carbon would save about 0.55 kg in total).
- **Hip spacer:** a printed horseshoe (RP-108, 35 mm thick, the full gap between the plates) ties the two thigh plates together around the hip, where one plate is on the hip-pitch actuator and the other on the knee actuator. Seven of the nine knee-actuator front screws pass through both plates and the spacer; the two lowest hold only the outer plate (shared 9-hole pattern). Two through-bolts at its leg ends replace the two upper standoffs. The bore (Ø56) and the open bottom clear the belt and the hip pulley.
- **Two knee drive variants, both kept:** the belt (above) and a linkage knee in the style of Unitree (`leg_linkage.sc`, `robot_linkage.sc`). The owner has not chosen between them yet.
  - **Linkage:** the knee actuator turns a 26 mm aluminium crank (RP-114). A Ø8 aluminium pushrod (RP-115) with an M5 rod end at each end runs down the rear of the thigh to a 34 mm lever on the shank above the knee axle (RP-116, printed). It is a four-bar: knee fold 45–140°, ratio 1.42:1 standing and at least 1.29:1 anywhere, rising to about 2.7:1 at the ends. Rod length sets the knee zero; there is no tensioner.
  - **Thinner thigh:** the plates (RP-111/112) taper from Ø84 at the hip to Ø36 at the knee, with a 20 mm gap instead of 35 (M3 × 20 standoffs, all in the front half). The hip spacer (RP-113) is a printed segment in front of the hip, clear of the crank. Knee axle RP-117.
  - **Results:** width over the knee actuators 303 mm (belt: 333); about 170 g lighter per leg (estimate). The hip carrier, actuators, foot pad, torso, neck, head and tail are shared with the belt variant.
- **New leg under study (motion rig only, not yet in the part files):** the owner is reshaping the linkage leg in `rig.js`, using the Unitree Go2 as the reference.
  - **Lengths:** thigh and shank 200/200 mm (the Go2 is 213/213), standing in the Go2's pose (hip 45.8°, knee −85.9°). The rig is about 370 mm tall, with the feet about 320 mm below the hip axes, roughly 15 mm behind them.
  - **Thigh:** two 3 mm aluminium plates shaped as a crescent of four tangent arcs: a hip round (R42), a knee round (R20), a convex rear edge (R300) and a concave front edge (R200). The folded shank therefore overlaps the thigh only near the knee. The rod runs inside the convex rear. Five standoffs (four behind the rod, one in front near the hip) and the hip spacer, trimmed to the concave front.
  - **Shank:** two 3 mm aluminium plates (26 wide) with spacers, nested inside the thigh fork. Each plate follows a curved centreline: straight from the knee leaning 8° forward, then an R172.5 arc that brings the foot back under the knee. The plate top is a round about the axle joined to a boss round the lever pin. The rod end is clamped between the plates (double shear).
  - **Knee:** fold 60–159°. At 159.8° the foot pad meets the thigh's hip end, so the lying-down pose has the feet against the hips. The fold starts at 60° rather than 50° to raise the knee ratio.
  - **Four-bar:** crank 22, lever 28 at −12° from the shank axis, rod lt + 3. Ratio 1.38 standing, 1.27–1.38 over the trotting folds (86–105°), at least 1.25, about 3.0 at 60° and 2.1 at 159°; transmission angles at least 18°. The crank can only sweep about 144°, so the ratio is set mainly by the fold range.
  - **Knee torque (hand estimate, 12.5 kg, the new leg):** RS02 actuator about 2.8 N·m standing, 10–11 N·m peak in a slow trot, 12–14 brisk, 14–16 fast, and about 5.3 N·m RMS in a slow trot (rated 6). The knee can deliver about 22–23.5 N·m (1.8 N·m per kg; the Go2 has about 3.0). Leg reach is about 346 mm fully extended, against 293 mm standing. With the old geometry (242 mm legs, 50–161°) the RMS was above the rating and brisk trots hit the 17 N·m peak.
- **Link lengths (part files and full robots):** thigh 242.2 mm (set by the belt; the linkage keeps it), shank 242 mm. Back height about 470 mm standing. The rig's 200/200 legs will replace these once the new leg goes into the part files.
- **Hip layout:** the thigh plane is 42 mm outboard of the abduction axis so it clears the abduction actuator and the torso. Abduction axes are 42 mm either side of the centreline. Hip pitch axes are 420 mm apart front to rear.
- **Width:** 333 mm over the knee actuators with the belt; 303 mm with the linkage (each 10 mm more than with the RS01, from the longer rear cover).
- **Torso:** each pair of abduction actuators is clamped between a bulkhead and a mid frame (3 mm aluminium). A printed belly pan spans between the mid frames; a 2 mm aluminium deck closes the top and extends as a spine to the neck and tail. Each spine end is stiffened by a bent 3 mm aluminium angle rib (front RP-205, 174 mm; rear RP-206, 125 mm, stopping 1 mm short of the tail wag servo), screwed to the deck along the centreline. The rib root passes through a slot in the bulkhead up to the mid frame. Lower corners are rounded about the abduction axes and the top is only 120 mm wide, so the thighs can swing past. The abduction actuators' plugs point straight up and down: they pass through a slot in the deck and a notch in the belly pan, and the mid frame has a notch and a tab under each actuator.
- **Knee direction:** all four knees bend backward.
- **Battery:** 13S2P Li-ion (owner's decision, 2026-11-21; replaces the 10S plan), using 26 high-drain 21700 cells (5 Ah, 25 A or more continuous). 46.8 V nominal, 54.6 V full, 39 V empty. 468 Wh nominal, about 375 Wh usable, about 2.1 kg (+1.3 kg over the old 10S1P plan). Estimated 1.7–2.8 h trotting. Estimated draw at 11 kg is 40–60 W standing, 120–200 W trotting and 0.5–1 kW peaks, scaled up with mass. The model still has the old 200 × 110 × 72 battery keep-out; resizing it is next (HANDOFF.md). Regen with a full pack can exceed the RS02's 60 V limit (braking resistor, or charge to 4.1 V per cell). Details and the 3P/4P comparison: `docs/battery.md`.
- **Shared parts across sides:** the assembly is mirrored left to right, but every fabricated part must be the same on both sides (owner's rule). Parts are symmetric or work turned over. The hip carrier has the actuator hole pattern every 60°, a plug slot top and bottom, and rear holes and head pockets for both hands, so one carrier fits all four hips.
- **Joint directions:** hip pitch and knee turn about +Y on every leg; positive abduction is outward on both sides. Actuator convention (true for the RS02): a dowel pin and a front M3 hole in line with the plug, M4 holes 30° off.
- **Mass:** target about 11 kg; current estimate 10.8–11.5 kg (the hip spacers and spine ribs added about 300 g; the head shell is about 230 g and the tail 137 g if solid; all of these should be lightened).
- **Joint limits found so far (all four legs driven together):** abduction outward about 17° for now, because the hip-pitch actuator's top plug swings into the deck spine from about 18° (the owner left the fix for later; the carrier itself meets the deck at about 32°); inward, the front and rear legs on the same side collide at 36°. Knee fold 145° with the belt (from the old model); 45–140° with the linkage in the full robot; 60–159° with the new leg in the rig.

## Tooling
- **Modelling rules** are in the `cad-modelling` skill (`.claude/skills/cad-modelling/SKILL.md`; the owner plans to move it to the personal skills folder). In short: one file per part, reuse by instancing, same parts on both sides, fully constrained sketches, one sketch and one hole feature per hole group, patterns and mirrors for repeats.
- **Models are generated, not hand-edited.** Node scripts in `cad/scripts/` write command scripts to `cad/*/build/` (git-ignored) and run them in SolidCraft. Run from the repo root:
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js all --app` builds every part, then all four assemblies and the motion rig. `parts <key>` builds one part; `leg`, `robot`, `leg_linkage`, `robot_linkage` or `rig` one assembly.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js symmetry [keys] --app` checks that every part used on both sides equals its own mirror image.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js check robot` (or any assembly key) runs a clash check on the saved assembly; with `--app` it also writes renders to its `build/` folder.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js pose [assembly] HipAbduction -45 45` drives that joint on all four legs to each angle and clash-checks that robot there (default `robot`). Without `--app` it runs one CLI script on the saved file and does not save it back.
  - `node cad/scripts/build.js ping [words] --app` tests the connection and lists app commands matching the words.
  - A part build fails if any sketch is not fully constrained.
- **How Claude reaches SolidCraft:** the CLI (`C:\Program Files\SolidCraft\solidcraft-cli.exe`) and the `solidcraft` MCP connector (a headless session; it can only open files inside the repo) both run now; Windows Smart App Control blocked them in earlier sessions because SolidCraft's Windows builds are unsigned (their issue #8317). Builds without `--app` use the CLI. `--app` instead sends the command scripts to the open desktop app over its local control channel (`cad/scripts/lib/control.js`; TCP port in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\SolidCraft\control\current.port`, with a token file next to it), which needs Preferences > Assistant > "Let AI agents connect" on. Each `--app` build runs in a new tab, saves, and closes that tab; the owner's tabs are left alone. Renders need the app or the MCP (`screenshot`).
- `.claude/settings.local.json` exempts `node cad/scripts/build.js *` from the Claude Code sandbox so the build can reach the app's port.
- The app re-saves every part file it rebuilds, and .sc files are binary, so a full rebuild shows every part as changed in git.
- **Generator files:** `dims.js` (every dimension, passed to the part files as named parameters), `parts.js` (one definition per part), `assemblies.js` (leg modules, both variants of the leg and robot), `rig.js` (the motion rig), `build.js` (runner), `lib/` (sketch helpers, placement maths, four-bar maths in `linkage.js`, control-channel client).
- **How assemblies are structured:** SolidCraft flattens a linked assembly file (its part list and joints are lost), so only part files are linked. The leg is defined once in `assemblies.js` as three rigid modules (hip, thigh, lower leg), plus a crank module and a rod module for the linkage variant. In the robot, modules are local sub-assemblies placed twice or four times: two hip modules and two thigh modules (one per hand), one lower leg. A right-hand module places the same part files in mirrored positions; the build refuses a mirrored part.
- **Linkage loop in SolidCraft:** crank–thigh and rod–crank are revolute joints, rod–lever a ball joint, made after the knee is driven to the standing pose (where the crank and rod were placed). Driving a knee moves the crank and rod; the crank angles match the four-bar maths to 0.01°. `joint.find_limits` stalls on the linkage (the rod ends touch the crank and lever face to face), so knee checks use discrete poses.
- **SolidCraft cannot drag grouped legs with the mouse (known limitation).** A click in the view, with any selection filter, picks the part inside a sub-assembly (for example LowerLeg:1 → ShankLk:1). The app then refuses the move silently ("no joint places it: it is not connected to anything grounded"), because it does not treat that part as moving with its parent's joints. Driving joints by value, and moving the sub-assembly itself (`joint.reach` on LowerLeg:1), both work. The same happens in the single-leg files. Only a flat layout (parts directly in the top assembly) would allow mouse dragging in SolidCraft; the owner rejected that for the real assemblies, so the motion rig below is a separate study model for dragging.
- **Motion rig (`cad/robot/motion_rig.sc`, built by `rig.js`):** the linkage-knee robot made to be dragged with the mouse, for finding joint limits, and now also where the new leg is designed (see Decisions). The torso is the real parts, linked into one grounded component. Each leg is five top-level components built in the file: hip (carrier and hip-pitch actuator with plugs, one definition for all four), thigh (crescent plates, spacer, standoffs, knee actuator), shank (two curved plates with their tops, axle tube, spacers, foot), crank and pushrod. Thigh and shank each have left and right definitions. The rig's leg lengths and four-bar are constants at the top of `rig.js` (`LT`, `LS`, `NL`), separate from `dims.js`. Limits: abduction ±45°, hip pitch ±120°, knee −159 to −60°. The crank and rod follow the knee through the four-bar. Saved in the Go2 standing pose (hip 45.8°, knee −85.9°). Parameters `lt`, `ls`, `lk_a`, `lk_b`, `lk_c` (= `lt` + 3) and `lk_d` (lever pin angle) can be changed in the app and the legs follow, but joint limits are plain numbers (the app does not re-read a limit expression). It is a study model: not in any BOM, and its handed links break the shared-parts rule on purpose (the real plates would serve both sides turned over).
  - **Live contact is too slow for it,** so the rig is saved with its "Collisions" contact set switched off. With contact on, every drag fails with "motion exceeds contact sweep intersection budget" after a freeze of several seconds, because jointed neighbours with sub-mm clearances slide past each other. Switch contact on in the app only to probe one limit. A one-off `contact.check` with the set enabled works but takes about 70 s. `build.js pose rig` switches contact off first in case it was saved on.
  - **Checking the new leg:** a 2D side-view checker in Python (shapely; written during the session, not in the repo) found the linkage, the free space for standoffs and the fold limit. `node cad/scripts/build.js pose rig Knee <angles>` then clash-checks the rig; with the current leg there are no clashes between links from −60 to −159°.
- **Four-bar maths (`lib/linkage.js`):** `knee(q, geometry)` and `ratio(q, geometry)` take an optional geometry (crank, lever, rod, lever angle, thigh length); without one they use the full robot's `dims.js` values. The rig passes its own.
- **Reading the owner's selection:** the control-channel method `ui.selection` returns what is selected in the open app (`selection.get` through `engine.execute` sees only the headless selection, which is empty).
- Named views (`view.apply {view: ...}`) frame the renders oddly; check the model visually in the app.
- Interference checks can run long: use `engine.batch` (one-hour timeout), not `engine.execute` (60 s).

## Repository layout
- `cad/parts/` – one design file per unique part (39 files: 29 for the belt robot, 9 added for the linkage knee, and the unused `robstride01.sc`, kept by the owner's choice), purchased parts and keep-out volumes included.
- `cad/leg/` – single-leg assemblies (`leg.sc` and `leg_linkage.sc`, front-left leg on a bulkhead), render and BOMs.
- `cad/robot/` – whole-robot assemblies (`robot.sc` and `robot_linkage.sc`, saved in the standing pose), the motion rig (`motion_rig.sc`), renders and BOMs (`bom.csv` and `bom_linkage.csv`, 27 items each).
- `cad/scripts/` – generators.
- `cad/actuators/` – older RobStride 01 reference model; the assemblies use `cad/parts/robstride02.sc`. `cad/actuators/build/` (git-ignored) holds local copies of the official RS01 and RS02 STEP files (licence not checked, so not committed).
- `docs/` – design notes: `robstride_comparison.md` (actuator specs, prices, purchase options, CAN vs CAN FD, RS02 fit check) and `battery.md` (13S2P pack sizing).
- **No production files in the repo** (owner's decision): DXF, 3MF and STEP exports go to `cad/*/export/`, which is git-ignored, and are only produced once the whole design is complete. The export step has not been rewritten for the new part files yet.
- Superseded, kept for now: `cad/leg/leg_module_concept.sc`, `cad/robot/robot_blockout.*`, `cad/scripts/gen_blockout.js`.

## Current state
First detailed pass, in linked part files. The whole robot is one articulated assembly (16 joints): a detailed torso, four detailed legs with real bolt patterns, and a neck, head and tail built around servo positions. It exists in two variants, belt knee and linkage knee. Every sketch is fully constrained and every part used on both sides passes the mirror-symmetry check. Nothing has been printed or cut.

In the latest session the model was switched to the RobStride 02 on all 12 leg joints, in both variants. The RS02 part was built from the official STEP file. This showed that the old RS01 model's front and rear screw patterns were 20° out of phase with its flange, so the thigh plates, hip spacers and bulkhead were drilled to a wrong pattern; all now follow the real one. The hip carrier, mid frame, deck and belly pan were changed for the longer rear cover and the plugs. Clash checks on both variants in the standing pose show only the known clashes, plus a 0.6 mm overlap between each abduction actuator's lower plug keep-out and the mid frame. Abduction poses were rechecked: outward, the hip-pitch actuator plugs now limit it to about 17°. The battery keep-out is still the old 10S one.

An earlier session added the motion rig so the owner can drag the legs. In the latest session the owner redesigned the leg in the rig only:
- 200/200 mm legs in the Go2 stance.
- A crescent thigh.
- A shank of two curved aluminium plates.
- A knee that folds to 159°, so the feet touch the hips when lying down.
- A four-bar retuned for a 60–159° fold, which raises the knee ratio to about 1.3–1.4 while trotting.

The part files and the full robots still have the old 242 mm linkage leg. Carrying the new leg into them is next (HANDOFF.md).

## Coordinate convention
X forward, Y left, Z up. Origin at the torso centre, at the height of the hip abduction axes. Leg-local frame: origin where the abduction axis meets the hip pitch axis, Y outward. Each part file has its own frame, described in a comment above the part in parts.js.
